text:
Accelerationism has evolved through distinct waves. Early iterations in the late 1960s and early 1970s involved French post-Marxists like Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, whose work, particularly the concept of "desiring-production," viewed desire as an inhuman flow of productive energy. This provided a framework for understanding capitalism as a radically deterritorializing process.
The concept was later popularized by Benjamin Noys to describe post-structuralists who embraced unorthodox Marxist views of capitalist growth. Later influential figures, such as Nick Land and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU), developed a more radical form, often characterized as a "technihilo" celebration of irrelevance of human agency, drawing inspiration from Nietzsche and Marxist concepts like the acceleration of class conflict. Modern iterations include "left-accelerationism," which seeks to accelerate past capitalism by democratizing productive technologies, and "right-wing accelerationism," which advocates for participating in capitalist growth to foster greater exponential change.
